review: Get lost for 2 hours on the same map until some random chinese dude show up and guide me all way to the end and crouching several times before leaving, absolute good game.
Literally just remnant 1 with Nothing but upgrades, improvements, and great additions, It is phenomenal and i cannot wait for any future content.

Short version. Game is a great 8.5/10 if you're on the fence for any reason, just dive off and give it a shot.

The good
Solid gameplay loop, decent story, amazing build diversity, immersive world supported by random generation and a fair few unique interactions which also generates a sizable amount of replayability. Rewarding exploration and choice (not just in dialog either)
No battle pass, no mtx, just a really great game in a box with some sweet DLC upgrades.
Plays great solo, and with friends.  I wish more people would play it.

The eh
Game doesn't do a fantastic job explaining itself, starting with difficulty scaling, stat details, how damage works, what does and doesn't count as what type of damage.  This isn't too much of an issue for most but can be an issue for some. 
Minimal character customization, 6 base faces, 6 voices, handful of skin, scar, hair options each for male and/or female.  This is made less important by armor options but the game also isn't trying to play fashion idol, some flare exists but largely the focus was on making the gameplay the reason to keep playing.

The 'bad'
You will eventually need to turn to 3rd party resources if you want to unlock everything.  There are a lot of items, and little story details you just aren't going to 'accidentally' discover.  Sure, you might stumble onto the alternate boss kill objective or get lucky and find an item before some npc gives you a quest to go get said item and this may change what you get as a reward, but then there are other, more creative unlock requirements you just won't ever figure out trying random things or exploring the far reaches.  (Lookin at you archon)  This isn't to take away from the work done to implement these things, in the case of the archon specifically I love why the unlock is the way it is, the dev's knew the kind of players they had and that is something to be praised.  However, not everyone likes or wants to keep a wiki open on the side to figure out how to get stuff. (But don't you lie to me, you've done it, I've done it, and as long as games keep including easter eggs and hidden loot, we're gonna keep doing it)

The controversial 
Hot take maybe, maybe not, I don't see a lot of discussion about this outside of what honestly feels like whining and self-reporting ignorance.  Anywho, I'm throw balance out there, as a somewhat bad item.
Not so much that it is unplayable by any means,  You can clear any boss/world on any difficulty with any combination of archetypes.  Buuuuuut, you're either lying to yourself or are just delusional if you think each archetype has the same power as any other.  Same for any weapon in the game.  Mostly this is a case of X just outshines A-V and Y or Z are only as good when used by/with one thing or another.  (probably one of the easiest examples of this is the comparison of the 'bulldog' vs the 'sparkfire', tell me one actually good reason to use the former over the later that ISN'T "because the bulldog is easier/faster to acquire", the sparkfire is just always better.)
This also looses some of it's bluster as an argument the higher the level in a way.  The gap in fun and power between the Invoker at level 1 to the Summoner at level 1 is much, much wider than it is when both are level 10.
But, as with anything said here, this is my opinion and not some gospel.  Even at their worst the 'bad' parts are more than made up for by the rest of the game, and honestly aren't even really that bad.  This is also before the final DLC drops which may or eliminate any of these points.

Anyway, get the game, try all kinds of stuff, hopefully have all kinds of fun and if not, at least you supported a good company trying to make good games still.

[h1] Remnant 2. [/h1]

• [h3] It's so good. [/h3]
A [b] "Souls-Like" [/b] game on Steam that finally deserves its place... a souls-like that does not aim to gate keep me with absurd difficulties or awful movement and combat when paired with a Keyboard\Mouse. Featuring secrets and treasures around every corner, exploring each tile set feels incredibly rewarding. A wonderful blend of looter-shooter stats and gearing to make build-making and endgame min-maxing feel diverse at every stage of your playthrough. Randomly generated world layouts to make every single player's first play-through completely different from someone else's.

Every core system of this game is incredibly well fleshed out, requiring some level of attention and knowledge from the player to help in learning build making, boss fighting, and world layouts.

• [h3] 'Dark Souls with Guns' [/h3]
As cringeworthy as this statement is these days, it does work as a description: Adding shooting to the genre really aids in the experience as a Keyboard\Mouse player, as I am always sick of the clunky movement and combat for the Standard Souls franchise. A classic gun and crosshair allow for another layer of game mastery and overall skill cap, which will be familiar to a lot of players. Remnant features a smooth and responsive gun playground for you to dodge, roll, and shoot things to your heart's content. Gun balance seems relatively well ironed out after the first few patches, and for your first few playthroughs, each gun shouldn't struggle with getting the job done until you are finally battling with Power Level 20 or Apocalypse Difficulty.

• [h3] Randomly generated dungeons and loot! [/h3]
Every playthrough will consist of five main areas. [spoiler] Yaesha, N'rud, Losomn, The Labyrinth, and Root Earth [/spoiler] as well as your main base of operations, Ward 13. Each 'world' has two main layouts, each with a set final boss. The journey towards the boss will be different in some way each time (bosses, loot, side areas, secrets, and side quests). Everything will be shifted around and repositioned on each playthrough. [u] Please understand. The game is meant to be played over and over again for full enjoyment. [/u]

• [h3] Build Engineering [/h3]
After my full time with the game, certain builds and formats saw repeated use of certain rings, and archetypes saw constant use compared to others, especially in the higher difficulties. But testing and making builds for your play style is entertaining and relatively in-depth for those willing to dig deep enough. But the topic of gear does push me towards the weakest aspect of the game, and that is in its comparison to the first game. Remnant [b] 1 [/b] Featured unique and interesting armour sets that granted bonuses depending on the amount of pieces equipped, they added just enough excitement and build diversity to make them worth looking at, but in Remnant 2 armour feels boring and thrown together poorly with nothing but a 'Weight\Armour' rating, with almost every player using either the lightest they can find or the heaviest with almost nothing in between. I truly hope armour gets more exciting down the line.

• [h3] Something for everyone [/h3]
I'll start by saying here that I don't often find myself enjoying Souls-like games for their awkward way of gatekeeping fun by locking the enjoyment behind dying to a boss 50 times over because of insane twists and absurd mechanics that one could only learn through experience, or a locked difficulty forcing you to play the game way all the time without the ability to mess around on an easier setting or without the ability to challenge yourself further. Remnant 2 offers four difficulties: [i] Survivor, Veteran, Nightmare, Apocalypse [/i]. I highly recommend starting this game on the lowest difficulty offered, especially if you want to play with friends, as the multiplayer scaling and latency can often be far too annoying to have to deal with a new mechanic on a higher difficulty. HP scaling is as follows: [i] 100%, 150%, 250%, 275% [/i] and damage scaling is: [i] 100%, 165%, 350%, 450% [/i]. As you can see, difficulties will spike your challenge dramatically, and the game itself recommends you only play on Nightmare+ if you have strong boss knowledge and build functionality. 

- 150 Hours Later
• Multiple Survivor Difficulty Runs
• Veteran, Nightmare, and Apocalypse Completion
• Hardcore Veteran Completion
• 100% achievement completion

[h1] 9.3 \ 10 [/h1]

Finally, a newly released game where I can happily say it's 'one of my favourites'. With the only issues being a few missing features that I wanted from the first game, the game shows fantastic polish, clear support from the development team with frequent patches and fixes, and a long road ahead of them with three promised DLCs to release the following year.

Do not be hesitant about trying out Remnant 2.
[spoiler] Feel free to ask questions about the game in the comments, or just bully me about writing too much. [/spoiler]

TL;DR: Fun and intense gunplay, excellent build variety, and tons of progression for neverending dopamine hits BUT reeeeaaally crap performance and tedious and illusory-wall-spamming “puzzles” gatekeeping unlocks. Bosses have many cancerous mechanics (e.g. half of them have instakill attacks), which is either a good or bad thing depending on how masochistic you are.

[hr][/hr]
[b][u]General Vibe[/u][/b]
Going through the biomes shooting and killing trash mobs is an absolute joy. Whenever an Elite spawns in the overworld, adds seemingly infinitely spawn until you take care of the Elite. Some players may dislike this (especially since those Elites don’t actively seek you out), but I enjoy this constant state of running and killing.

However, there are a few questionable design choices. Dodging, vaulting, AND jumping from ledges are all on the same button. Feels annoying to climb over cover you want to dodge into.

Also, there isn’t an interaction key for ladders—nor is there a way to animation cancel once you’ve started mounting one. This means if you so much as touch a ladder, you are locked into an animation where enemies are free to attack you.

[b][u]Performance[/u][/b]
I’m running a GTX 1080 (stronger than the supposedly “recommended” RTX 2060 as per the Steam Store page) and playing on 1080p 60FPS with everything on the absolute lowest settings. Despite that, I’m having massive frame issues in half the biomes and parts of the hub. Other users are reporting similar issues.

I will say that Remnant 2 on lowest settings looks just as good as Remnant 1 on highest settings, so it’s not the worst. Once patches fix the frame issues, we’re good to go.

[b][u]Builds[/u][/b]
By far the best part of Remnant 2. While the unique armour effects from Remnant 1 are gone, most of their effects have shifted to Mutators you can slot onto your weapons. On top of that, you have alternative Relics (i.e. Remnant’s Estus Flask equivalent), stat sticks to place on your Relics, Mods to slot into your weapons, an Amulet slot, 4 Ring slots, many Archetypes to select, and 3 Skills per Archetype to customise your character.

There are also DPS dummies in the hub to test out your damage, which is nice.

What's controversial is how Remnant 2 changed Traits, which are small incremental increases for stats like health and movement speed. In Remnant 1, Trait points were unlimited: with both DLCs, you could have a level 1,000 maxed out character. In Remnant 2, you are limited to a max of 60 out of 300-ish (85 if you're using 2 level 10 Archetypes).

The principal designer has stated this change was made to improve build diversity and make it easier to balance future content. I'm neutral on this change, though many players absolutely hate it.

[b][u]Bosses[/u][/b]
People HATED the add spam in Remnant 1, and the devs have taken that feedback into account. Adds are no longer a constant horde—the bosses that spawn adds often perform an animation to signal that they’re summoning, and the adds that appear are usually limited to a handful.

HOWEVER.

They have given the bosses tons of cancerous mechanics. Those who have played Remnant 1 will remember Enchanter Shroud. Imagine that design philosophy applied to every boss that has a modifier. [strike]My favourite new addition is the modifier that heals the boss for a third of their HP whenever you use a Relic, which is more of an ammo-check than anything else.[/strike] They nerfed this. :(

Also, why do half of the bosses have instakill attacks? Especially the cubes. What the fuck is that?

Now, I’m a masochist who appreciates bullshit unfair fights in my Soulslikes, so I LOVE this. Others may not. 

[b][u]Puzzles[/u][/b]
The “puzzles” in Remnant 2 are designed with Google Search in mind, and it shows. Some of the unlocks are only discoverable with thousands of players sharing info after one randomly lucked into the solution.

If you like puzzles, you’ll get annoyed at how lethal some of the puzzles are—there are now runbacks for fucking puzzles. I don’t mind trial-and-error, but when some puzzle runbacks are longer than Elden’s Ring’s Placidusax runback, it’s just disrespectful of the player’s time.

Not to mention some puzzles take a 90 IQ person 10 seconds to figure out but require 20 minutes of boring running back and forth to complete. And let’s not forget the Goddamn illusory walls. It’s the laziest form of “puzzle” in Soulslikes, and it forces players to either a) dodgeroll into every fucking wall or b) have to look up guides to find items. There are also puzzles that require multiple players, so enjoy begging in the Discord.

And if you hate puzzles and just want to experiment with builds and shoot things, have fun with how often you have to tab out to Google how to open a locked door.

I’m not expecting this game to be like Portal, but it feels like half of the more complex unlocks are from the Genshin Impact School of haha le rand0m, with the other half being from the Elden Ring Academy of Illusory Walls.

[b][u]Overall[/u][/b]
Remnant 2 is great. Gameplay is extremely satisfying, and boss fights are brutally fun. Performance is currently crap, and there are a few bugs here and there, but nothing a few patches won’t fix. Excited for what’s to come.

As a casual gamer, I often look for games that offer both an engaging experience and the flexibility to not consume all my spare time. Remnant 2 has hit that sweet spot perfectly, making it a must-play title in my collection. Here’s why I think it’s a fantastic game, especially if you're not a hardcore gamer but still crave a deep and satisfying experience.

One of the standout features of Remnant 2 is its co-op gameplay. Teaming up with friends or even online strangers to tackle challenges together adds an extra layer of enjoyment and accessibility. The co-op element is seamlessly integrated, making it easy to drop in and out of games without disrupting the flow. This flexibility is perfect for someone like me, who may not have long hours to dedicate in one sitting. It’s also a great way to share the fun and strategies with buddies, enhancing the overall gaming experience.

What I appreciate most about Remnant 2 is its challenging nature, which is finely balanced to be accessible yet stimulating. The game scales its difficulty based on the number of players, so whether I’m solo or with friends, the challenge feels just right. This adaptability keeps the gameplay fresh and engaging. Each enemy and boss fight tests your skills and strategies but isn’t so tough that it becomes a frustrating grind. This makes every victory satisfying without being overly taxing, which is perfect for players who aren’t looking for an ultra-hardcore experience.

Exploring the world of Remnant 2 is an adventure in itself. The game boasts a rich narrative that unfolds as you traverse through diverse and beautifully crafted environments. Each area is unique, with its own set of mysteries and lore, encouraging exploration and interaction. The story is deep and well-integrated into the gameplay, providing context and motivation behind the battles and challenges. It’s this blend of story and exploration that keeps the game intriguing and makes each session feel like a new discovery.

On top of all that, their release of excellent quality DLC takes me back to the days when Game Developers used to care and provide quality.

Overall, Remnant 2 is a brilliantly crafted game that caters wonderfully to both casual and seasoned gamers. Its co-op play is a blast, the challenges are perfectly paced, and the rich world is full of stories and sights that are captivating. For anyone looking for a game that offers more than just mindless action but is still approachable for a casual gaming session, Remnant 2 is a stellar choice. Whether you’re exploring dark, mysterious settings or taking down giant bosses with friends, Remnant 2 provides a rewarding experience that’s hard to put down. Highly recommended for those looking for a game that’s as enjoyable as it is engaging!

Let me start off by saying, I absolutely love this game. I am 15 hours into the game on Veteran and i'm only just now on the second world. While there's so much good to say about this game I do think there are a few glaring issues as well.

Pros:
-It is an absolutely breathtaking world full of lore. A lot of areas appear to be influenced by other main stay souls games such as bloodborne and Dark Souls. But you also have completely new looking areas that are just as visually stunning.
-There are so many ways to play and so many variations to builds, you could easily put in 100 hours just trying to test multiple builds.
-An amazing gameplay loop that makes it easy to continue playing the game without getting bored.
-They carried over the ability from the first game to reroll you're campaign, so if you're looking to fight every boss this game has to offer and find every secret, get ready to stop, drop and reroll.

Cons:
-I'll start with the easiest one to point out. Optimization. The game does have pretty poor optimization which can hold it back a bit. My system is about mid tier and I can't really play unless my upscaler is on performance mode unless I want to sit at 30 frames the entire time. A buddy of mine has a 3080 and it's chugging along at max settings. This is just a word of caution though.
-The biggest issue with this game I believe is scaling though. While the game has a lot of variety, you won't really get to use it because of scaling. If you have +10 weapons, you better hope that you have enough scrap to get whatever new weapon you want up to +10 before using it. This however leads into the next issue though.
-Removal of key features from the first game feels devastating. The fact that I can't level up my armor anymore just feels awful. While everything is scaling up damage and health, I can really only scale up my damage unless I want to drop points into vigor which doesn't do too much. The better armor you get, the higher the weight, so now you're only options are high armor high weight (crappy dodging) or low armor low weight (good dodging) instead of being able to level up an armor set in order to keep low weight with high armor. There's also the removal of gear set bonuses which might just be a personal gripe for me but I really enjoyed those in the first game. Added extra flavor to each build.

This game can be challenging, but fun. However, we ran into a big game-breaking bug.

My problem so far (6 hours in for them), is that you can lose most or all of your progress just because. We played for hours yesterday, came to a good stopping point, logged off, went to bed, hopped back on and one of our friends (the host) had their character and world reset. 

When looking for solutions, it became clear logging in with all progress being lost is a major well-known issue that could happen under many different circumstances (including your game crashing). There is 1 recommended solution and nothing else. These posts were dated 2-3 years ago.

Our run was pretty smooth. We got to the Ward, went to a world, defeated some bosses, explored some areas, went back to Ward, made some purchases and logged off. 

When our friend logged back in, it didn't start them where it should've. It didn't start at the tutorial with Ford either (which can happen). It put them in an entirely new world, with a level 1 character with none of the weapons, armor, etc. that we got from the night before. The character has the same archetype but, that's it. They did NOT re-roll the campaign either. All of it is gone. 

When attempting to do the recommended backup and cloud save backup fix, the most recent backup save either way was at the intro/character creation so, it would be the same as starting over, which is the only other "fix". There are no manual saves for this game. 

In this game, you have to touch a World Stone to save. We did this multiple times throughout our playthrough. Our friend's backup saves didn't capture any of those World Stone points. 

There were no patches pushed that could've created this issue (which is also well known). No network issues. No crashes. No prompts for a re-roll. No new game. Seemingly no recent save data points backed up somehow over the course of 6 hours.

The devs have moved on from this game so, if this happens to you, you're out of luck. 

I appreciate that they have the save files in more than 1 place, but, if that was your solution, you needed to make sure it was developed properly. How this kind of defect made it past QA is unacceptable.

It's an okay game if you play it casually with some friends. The core gameplay loop of a single playthrough is alright, even if the story isn't as interesting as the first game. 
The reason this is a negative review is that it sucks to play if you either: Don't have all the dlc, or if you ever look up something online. Let me explain:

The DLC issue - Don't you love beating that cool looking boss and wondering what interesting new loot it will drop? Well too bad. Even with just completing the first world of the game once, there were two bosses that dropped DLC-locked loot. It's the most unsatisfying feeling to beat a challenging boss and then find out it gave you nothing because you didn't buy the Ultimate edition. And, as you can't sell certain types of loot, you get the constant reminder that you don't own the dlcs by seeing a crossed out loot in your inventory every time you open it.

Looking things up - I don't mind puzzles, and most of the mandatory puzzles in the game are alright. Having a few challening puzzles isn't a problem. It is however a problem when the playerbase couldn't even find out that an entire archetype exists until it was datamined out of the game. I get the point of having secrets, but come on. Making the player stand still in a corner of a random room for five minutes is not an engaging way to unlock a new archetype (I am not kidding, that's how the Invoker class is unlocked) I don't want to have five pages of guides open just to get a singular weapon. A lot of loot and unlocks are also tied to "events" which have a random chance of occuring in certain areas when certain conditions are met. As they have a random chance of occuring; it gives the very challenging and engaging gameplay loop of resetting an area twenty times until the event spawns. 

The core gameplay is fine, but the painstaking process of needing several pages of guides or being dlc-locked out of loot in the base game has soured my experience in a way i never expected. If you want to enjoy yourself then I recommend never looking up a single guide or wiki-page about the game,. You don't need the extra stuff to beat the game, and it is not worth it to open pandoras box just for a gun that you probably don't even enjoy using more than what you already have.

Having upscaling is great. 

But requiring upscaling for playable performance on high end GPUs is a joke. Especially if the visuals don't warrant it.

Remnant 2 is a really good game with a whole lot to do.  If you are a recovering Destiny player like myself and looking for something similar but more challenging, you have found it.  Also, it has a dog and you can pet it.  I only have the base game, so my review is just that with no expansions added in.

Why would you want to play this game instead of Destiny?  Its not a looter shooter.  It has snappy gunplay, a great sci-fi storyline, a lot of build diversity, and maps you can replay.  When you defeat a final world boss, you can craft it into a gun.  It also has co-op if you are into that, I am not. It reminds me a lot of soloing 3 man content in Destiny, which is why I bring that up!

The main draw here is the world "Reset" features.  So there's 3 modes: Campaign, Adventure, and (as of this week) Boss Rush.  You can play each mode independently of the others and with different difficulties.  When done with a mode because you've finished it or just want to try something else, you can just re-roll a new one.  If playing Campaign or Adventure, you will get a different storyline for each world when you do this, which keeps it fresh.  Each individual rolled world is made of semi-randomized maps.  From what I can tell, the expansions add more storylines to choose from as well as new classes and weapons.

I played the the first one, Remnant: From the Ashes last year.  This game is just straight up better, the maps are in general more interesting.  My main gripe with the first game is that a lot of the bosses just felt like bullet sponges to wait out.   They addressed that in this game by giving each boss its own puzzle element.  That turned me off initially, but I grew to like it.  So for example, one of the bosses is floating in the center of its arena.  After you get past a certain health threshold, it will go immune and it will destroy the part of the arena you are standing in; and you if you are there.  Most of them are not more complex than that.  There is the now-famous cube boss also, which is just straight up a puzzle.  So that puzzle aspect does also mean that some of the bosses have instant-kill effects.  This can cause issues when doing boss rush if you are not familiar with that boss.

As for difficulty, it has options.  The Survivor is "easy", Veteran is intended for players starting fresh, Nightmare is for players that have leveled up and have gear and a build, and Apocalypse is for folks who want a challenge after finishing the campaign at least once.  Normally I just ratchet the difficulty up, but that felt like a waste of time just starting out.  So I did the campaign in Veteran, and rolled a few adventures in Nightmare.  I just finished the game so I have not been able to check out Apocalypse yet.  The higher difficulties award more xp and crafting materials, which you use to make weapons and mods.  It does have archetype level and weapon difficulty scaling inside of each mode, which caps out at 20.  In the first game, there was a whole meta around keeping your weapons un-upgraded until encountering the boss; that's not worthwhile in this game.

There are some bugs.  I didn't encounter anything game-breaking, just annoying.  I played Summoner for a while, and the summons would not change zones or go through doors with me consistently.  So I typically ran into the bossfight and summoned instead of dealing with that, which consumes a percentage of your health.  I didn't have issues with the Handler class' dog so it seemed strange.  Also there were a couple of times that I could not interact with the thing I needed to interact with.  Leaving and coming back fixed that.  

Do be aware that if you are an achievement hunter, there are achievements tied directly to expansion content.

With great excitement, I spent time playing the game with a friend until we hit the first grind cap. When we were up against one of the penultimate bosses, we simply didn't have enough damage. Even as a healer, I couldn't constantly keep healing and reviving the damage dealer [i](it seems the talent for faster revives glitched, as I couldn't level it up in a co-op session)[/i]. As a result, we embarked on adventures, farmed another bunch of rings and scrap, but most importantly, we upgraded our weapons and progressed further.

Am I understanding correctly that everyone tackles the final boss solo? [i](At least today a patch was released that balances this aspect)[/i]

The final boss is the epitome of challenge and difficulty. It seems they even buffed it after the last patch [i](before 08.10.23 patch)[/i], as "circles" now appear "unlinked," making it practically impossible to shoot them all down. We spent two sessions of four hours each on it. We tried everything under the sun; the last attempt was a build focused on maximum healing and shields, plus revives and two of each ability. We didn't progress past 1.5 phases. We simply lacked damage. Strangely, the boss aggroed the host player 95% of the time, which meant the tank had to deal damage, while the damage dealer was running around wounded. Honestly, I didn't want to give up on the game; I wanted to finish it. Eventually, I gave in and decided to level up my "sniper" weapon, as my "+20 Thompson" was useless against this boss, who spent most of the time at a distance. For some reason, I had initially thought that I needed to focus on leveling up submachine and machine guns as my main weapons (and also double-barreled shotgun). In the end, after maxing out my sniper riffle, we defeated the boss after 30 minutes of attempts.

I must admit, after a couple of days of attempts and additional resource farming, I still remained satisfied.

The only thing is, I never quite understood who the close combat weapon class is aimed at, considering that the majority of the game involves fighting at a distance, and getting up close tends to result in a beating. I won't say I didn't enjoy the challenge of grinding levels, but this fact did frustrate me a bit; essentially, you're required to grind for upgrades or even classes. The game doesn't seem to allow you to complete it the way you want. I don't have that much time [i](or desire)[/i] for such activities. Perhaps I'm to blame for choosing the veteran difficulty and not being a fan of "build making". However, in the first game, which we completed multiple times, I didn't encounter such issues. Also, the talent level cap also steers the game more toward build making and carefully analyzing numbers and meta [i](At a difficulty level above veteran)[/i].

But I came here for an adventure with my friend, and in principle, I got that. The sequel turned out to be what it should be: the same game but with more content. The game is particularly rich in secrets and interesting bosses [i](though not always fair)[/i]. Unfortunately, my brainpower and patience weren't enough to truly decipher them, but my friend remained satisfied and honestly tried to figure them out [i](while I watched walkthroughs on YouTube)[/i]. During our playthrough, we rerolled the adventures 5-6 times, and we still stumbled upon previously undiscovered locations. Every time I thought we were done, that we had seen everything, my friend would tell me about a couple more items or bosses.

I put a lot of time into Remnant 2, and it genuinely surprised me with how deep and replayable it turned out to be.

The main and sub-class (archetype) system is the standout. Being able to mix and match archetypes completely changes how the game plays, and it never felt like there was just one “correct” setup. Swapping combinations opened up new strategies, new synergies, and made experimenting feel rewarding instead of risky.

I was especially impressed that summoning was introduced. Running builds that revolve around summons added a whole new layer to combat and made encounters feel more dynamic. It wasn’t just a gimmick either—the summons felt meaningful, useful, and well integrated into the overall systems.

Replayability is where the game really shines. Between randomized worlds, different archetype combinations, and alternative approaches to encounters, every new run felt distinct. Even after finishing a playthrough, I kept coming back to try new builds and paths just to see how differently things could play out.

Overall, Remnant 2 nails that sweet spot: deep customization without being overwhelming, surprising systems like summoning done right, and enough variety to keep you hooked across multiple runs. It’s the kind of game that rewards curiosity and keeps pulling you back in.

[b]After sinking more than 150 hours into Remnant 2, clearing the campaign multiple times on the hardest difficulty, and even beating Hardcore mode, I feel confident enough to share my thoughts.[/b]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Story[/h2]
The campaign is designed to feel fresh every time. Thanks to the game’s use of tile sets for events, dungeons, and story beats, no two playthroughs are exactly alike. Every run feels like a unique adventure.

While the overall main story might not blow everyone away, the individual world stories are where this game shines. Each map has its own lore, characters, and choices that directly affect your rewards. Don’t skip the dialogue—your decisions matter, and replaying arcs with different choices lets you unlock alternative rewards.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Maps[/h2]
The maps are absolutely gorgeous and incredibly well-crafted. Each one feels alive and distinct, from magical forests and regal palaces to ghost towns and desolate alien worlds. They’re packed with unique enemies, hidden rewards, and tons of secrets and easter eggs waiting to be discovered. Exploring each location is an experience on its own.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Combat[/h2]
The combat is “soulslike” in spirit but much more accessible once you get the hang of it. Gunplay feels tight and satisfying, melee combat is equally solid, and dismembering enemies adds a nice punch to encounters. Best of all—it doesn’t fall into the bullet sponge trap that many games suffer from. Once you grind and build up your character, you really feel powerful enough to take on whatever the game throws at you.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Classes (Archetypes)[/h2]
One of the game’s coolest features is the dual-class system. You can equip two archetypes at once, mixing their abilities for unique playstyles. You start with one class, but others can be unlocked as you progress through the worlds. There’s a lot of build variety here, which keeps things exciting even on repeat playthroughs.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Weapons & Mods[/h2]

[b]Weapons[/b] come in three categories:

i.[b]Long Guns:[/b] ARs, DMRs, shotguns, LMGs, bows, railguns, crossbows, disk launchers, and more.

ii.[b]Handguns:[/b] Pistols, revolvers, SMGs, sawed-off shotguns, grenade launchers, elemental weapons, and some wild hybrids (like the [i]Anguish[/i], a shotgun-SMG-explosive combo).

iii.[b]Melee:[/b] Swords, scythes, hammers, axes, and unique tools like the [i]Dreamcatcher[/i], which lets you literally enter the dreams of NPCs and enemies.

[b]Mods[/b] are another highlight—they attach to weapons and grant powerful, unique abilities that can change how you approach fights.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Replayability & Community[/h2]
This game has insane replay value. Between the randomization, multiple paths, and build variety, every run feels different. Plus, the community is super helpful, always ready to guide new players.

Performance has been solid for me too. Across 150+ hours, I’ve only had one or two crashes, and frame rates are stable (though your mileage may vary based on hardware).

If you’re considering buying, I [i]strongly recommend[/i] the [b]Ultimate Edition[/b]. It adds meaningful content and tile sets to the game, and the price difference is small—especially on sale. Unlike many other games, here the higher edition actually adds real value.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Cons[/h2]
As much as I love this game, it does have one glaring weakness: social features. There’s no text chat or in-game voice chat, which makes playing with randoms a bit rough.
There is a funny workaround though—the Long Gun [i]Monolith[/i] can be used to draw text on walls, letting you share friend codes or basic messages with teammates. Creative, but not ideal.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Final Verdict[/h2]
[i]Remnant 2[/i] is a polished, content-rich, and endlessly replayable co-op shooter that combines challenging combat, great build variety, and some of the best procedural storytelling I’ve seen. Despite the lack of proper communication tools, I’d still call this a 10/10 must-play for anyone who loves third-person shooters, co-op adventures, or soulslike games.

So overall I think Remnant 2 has great potential and could be better than the first game, but there are some key issues with it. 

- First you can't upgrade armor, only weapons/mutators. (The previous game you could upgrade armor up to +20)

- You are capped at 60 Trait Points, each Trait has 10 levels so you can max out 6 traits. (The previous game had no cap you just had thousands of points you could potentially spend.)

- You don't gain Trait Points for leveling up anymore, you only get XP for your Archetype (Class), you can only have 2 classes equipped at any given time so there is little point to leveling up the other classes. Yes you unlock the Class Trait for all classes but again you are capped at 60 points so its an option that doesn't mean anything because you can't take it. 

- So at a certain point there is no benefit for fighting enemies, fighting bosses, or exploring the world because the only thing you get from it is money. You can max out your weapons, your classes and your trait points which means progression stops cold. You can unlock more items and traits but you are capped on how much of those you can use so if you are building your character a certain way that means these are useless unless they are better than what you already have. You are capped on your equipment slots, you are capped on your classes, you are capped on your upgrades, and you are capped on your traits. All in all some of these make sense, equipment, classes, and upgrades make sense, but the traits don't. This is what made the first game so much fun was that even if it was small progression you constantly made progression and Remnant 2 has ruined that.

- The previous game had nearly endless replay ability because you could always level  up and gain more traits, there were dozens of traits to unlock through various methods, you had randomized maps so there were a lot of maps you could miss on your first couple of play-throughs, and there alternate items for a lot of the bosses so you'd need to fight them again to get everything. Also there were items you could only get on certain difficulties, so that added a whole new layer to this.  

- The game is way harder than the previous one, I wouldn't normally view that as an inherently bad thing but with the fact that you have hard caps on your avatar strength makes it so. Armor feels very flimsy and the 2nd best armor in the game only reduces damage by around 30-40%. In return you get some of the worst dodges in the game. I get that's a trade off but Remnant 1 made that transition very well because once you hit a certain Avatar Strength level is made more sense to increase the difficulty to maintain the Souls-Like experience. Remnant 2 doesn't do that, and because of that the armor doesn't have a good enough effect for the limited dodge to be worth it. Why would I increase the difficulty if my existing armor feels like toilet paper and my avatar strength has been capped on my first play thru?

- Remnant 2 is very close to being a good game, but some key design choices have ruined that potential. There is DLC planned for the game but there isn't a point to going thru it if I have the best build for what my character is supposed to be built for. I can experience the story, but Remnant 1 was a game that had a story but the story itself wasn't ground breaking or life changing. It was a solid story for a 3rd person shooter RPG. The point of the game was the RPG Souls-like experience. Yes players could get more powerful and the souls-like would slowly fade but thats what the higher difficulties were for, so you could play a harder game for what you want out of it. This is why games like Borderlands maintain a longer audience because there is constant small progression in the end game.

This game has a multitude of annoyances and bad design that make it very hard to commit to this game unless you and your friends aren't taking it all to seriously. I mean, seriously, the amount of content in this game that you will miss on one playthrough is INSANE because the Devs want to give players incentive to replay this. The only problem is that the replayability past the first playthrough is a major annoyance and a dry husk.

First of all, the levels you and your party will go through are all randomly generated, and no matter what you do, On a first playthrough, you will always miss content and bosses due to how the devs designed the game. Weapons, Armor, and even Classes will be potentially locked from you unless you go back to redo these levels over and over again for the things that you want. On top of all that, some of these weapons, mods, and armors require certain knowledge in order to obtain them. Problem with that is there is almost ZERO way for you to figure any of that out midgame, and most of it involves the average player looking back and forth between the wiki to see how and more importantly, when they can obtain such an item. These requirements can range from collecting a key item and using it during a boss fight or interaction that has no hints or buildup leading to it, or focusing the body part of a specific boss that ALSO gives no hint or buildup towards. It's bad design, especially if your really hoping for 'your' kind of weapon and end up not getting it until your at the final boss and finally start questioning where all the weapons are.

As stated above, lots of content it barred until a second playthrough.. and the DLC's don't make it any better. Most of the DLC's require you to replay the game AGAIN just to access the content related to it. It's absurd just how much boring and dull repeatability the Devs try and shove into your face through this experience. Speaking of which, the game is extremely punishing for people who miss this opportunity as you will lose out on classes, weapons, and etc for not doing the very specific requirements for them, that you have no way of realistically knowing due to how the game is structured in bringing forth information.

Contrary to what I said in the beginning, despite this being a good Co-Op experience, it is not a good game when it comes to combating anything but bosses. You are mostly just drilling rounds into enemies with almost no recoil and the build customization makes your build in the most standard way 'do more damage' without adding any actually engaging combat design. Classes is where that unique combat shines but no matter what you do it's the same formula. 

Overall, I would not recommend getting this game until a very generous sale comes along. Play this with two other friends for the best experience if that were to happen. IF this game does get another installment of the series, I severely hope they will stop with the repeatability nonsense and make ALL the content accessible in one play through.

But after 8 hours the game somehow managed to click with me: bosses were extremely fun, amazing balance of unique design, gimmick and difficulty.

I really can't stress how impressed I am with Remnant 2--it is exceedingly rare that sequels truly honor originals, but this game takes it to another level. 

The attention to detail and characterization of the world design is so unreal, and there are hidden secrets and areas all over the place. If Remnant 1 felt like Dark Souls simply meets guns, Remnant 2 feels like Dark Souls meets Time Splitters 2. There's a soul to each world with their story to be felt, there are interesting enemy designs and challenging, glorious boss fights, and there are new classes and archetypes to keep you engaged through the grind.

It's just very refreshing to see developers learn all of the right lessons from their first game and then simply make a direct improvement in almost every way. Save whatever performance issues other people seem to be having, I really can't find much to complain about whatsoever. Nicely done devs, this is a real sequel.

OK, this game is good. I enjoy it. I'll keep playing it. Certain parts, like the loadouts and expanded jewelry list feel really good, and the archetypes are really interesting. But I'm very disappointed - its just not as fun nor as good as Remnant 1, especially for long-term replayability or even just game design. I think patches could repair many of these issues, so please keep an eye on what they do with this game over the next year. But I'm disappointed I pre-ordered this game thinking it would build on the good parts of the prequel. All my complaints below are introduced in Remnant 2. 
- Stability issues: It crashes often, experiences memory leaks, lags with crazy lag spikes even at the lowest graphic settings on a 3070ti. 
- Gameplay restrictions: Melee is not viable. In remnant 1, only two bosses fly out of reach. In this game, nearly every boss is flying out of reach. The few who aren't flying have an insta-kill melee attack, so you don't want to be near them (insta-kill is not good game design...). Additionally, almost every region has common flying enemies or explosion on death effects, so even open world melee feels bad.
- No survival mode: Remnant 1's best replayability was survival mode (rogue-like, find the game's jewelry and see how many bosses you can beat). This game entirely misses it. But, with the boss difficulty so much higher in this game, I don't even know if its viable. Remnant 1 bosses could be beaten reliably once you're good at the game. This game introduces insta-kills to boss fights, and often unavoidable deaths with the sheer number of hitboxes or enemies in boss fights. IMO, that doesn't make it more fun.
- Weirdly Balanced: Certain min/max builds severely outpace any casual or fun build. With the increased difficulty and high health pools of enemies, this makes casual/fun builds feel too difficult to play, and many interesting jewelry don't get used.
- Far less replayability: I'm amazed that, after my first playthrough, I'm getting so many repeat jewelry/weapon pickups (purple items turning to scrap). The areas in each region repeat so often, and the jewelry that appear in those regions are static, meaning the second playthough doesn't feel much different than the first. Mix that with the 65 trait cap, why would I continue playing the game? Leveling up archetypes is also pretty quick, so where's the added benefit beyond grinding to upgrade my weapons? Mix this with the lack of survival mode that I mentioned before, and I struggle to convince myself to keep playing. I've dumped hundreds of hours in remnant 1 and continue to do so; yet after 50 in this "highly replayable" game, I'd seen enough. That's crazy for a sequel that promises more equipment, jewelry, content etc! I'm amazed we still only have 3 worlds to explore - that's less than remnant 1 even before it's DLC! And the upcoming remnant 2's first DLC isn't adding a world??
- Menuing feels so much worse - why did you have to add so many more button clicks to put on mods and gear? Why take away the table format from remnant 1 where I could at least see ring names/details, where now I need to memorize ring images to remember what each one does? Especially prevalent on the shards you add to the relics; blue/red/yellow being the only visible information is insane.

Gunfire games, I don't know what changed about your vision, but it feels like you wanted to make this game more souls-like in a stand-back-and-fire gameplay. So many boss attacks feel un-dodge-able (ex: multi-hit where dodging the first hit means the second hit clips you). Other boss attacks do unnecessary amounts of damage. and what's with the insta-kills? Remnant 1 played more like an arcade shooter with just enough difficulty sprinkled in, works in melee/short-range/long-range. The ability to swap between different styles of gameplay based on the build is what made remnant 1 so good and replayable. This game feels like that excellent balance and design was tossed out the window.

I really liked Remnant 2 overall. I played through the game on Veteran difficulty and honestly, the gameplay is probably the strongest part of it. The gunplay feels even smoother than Remnant 1, the weapons have more impact, and the movement and combat just feel really good. Shooting, dodging, switching weapons and messing around with different builds is genuinely fun.

But man, the optimization is rough. Some areas run perfectly fine and then you enter certain DLC maps and the performance just falls apart. The random stutters and FPS drops really take away from the experience, especially during fights where every frame matters.

Another thing I really wish they did better is the bosses. I'm not even comparing them to other Soulslikes, but after beating a lot of the bosses, I rarely got that "holy sh*t, I actually did it" feeling. Some fights are cool mechanically, but none of them felt truly iconic or memorable to me. I wish the bosses had more personality and those moments that stick with you long after the fight is over.

The story is also nothing special, and the procedural nature of the game can sometimes make exploration feel a little repetitive. The progression and traits aren't always that exciting either.

Still, I'd recommend Remnant 2. The core gameplay is just too much fun to ignore. It has some rough edges, but when everything clicks, it's a really damn good shooter.

Remnant 2 is definitely not a bad game. It plays very similarly to the first game but with more focus on class roles versus just general equipment. With your classes determining your playstyle and ability, it makes for some very interesting combinations. At first I was extremely disappointed I could not don the full cultist set and spam the bubble shield with hunters mark, but as I progressed I found the many minor perks you gain from your classes more than make up for the lack of armor bonuses. As I entered the lategame a plethora of options opened to me, and my build became genuinely fun to play. This game starts off like shit, I won't sugarcoat it. The story is contrived and the voice acting is decent at best, but the actual gameplay is where it shines. The addition of a wide variety of dragon hearts is quite a cool touch, but somewhat lackluster when you consider 90% of them are niche at best, and genuinely unusable at worst. I feel Remnant 2 plays smoother and more diversely than the first game, in terms of build quality and abilities, but certain "improvements" feel rather lacking. The minimap is god awful, bugging out and looking like shit; occasionally it decides a portion of land simply does not exist, or to get stuck at max zoom despite my efforts to move it out even slightly. Certain items are locked behind getting lucky with multiple layers of RNG tied to the main campaign, which I am not a fan of but begrudgingly grind out regardless. The final boss fight, however, was an experience to be sure. It has mechanics that I personally quite enjoyed and would place in my top 10 coolest boss fights solely because of 1 mechanic, ignoring the visuals included. I loved every second of the fight and it was truly a grand battle to finish out my journey. Unfortunately, the final boss of the DLC was a complete pushover. A friend and I with half-completed builds (we swapped off DOT builds to preserve his hammer for an alt boss kill reward) managed to beat the One True King first try on apocalypse difficulty. He had perhaps one threatening attack, which was quite literally just a massive AOE with maybe a 0.5 second windup. The gun you gain from killing him (alt kill where you don't break his hammer; yes that is genuinely a challenge it just takes damage as he uses it) is probably the coolest weapon I've used in both games, featuring an auto homing mode. That being said, it is close in terms of DPS and general playstyle/build to the Chicago typewriter (my beloved).

tl;dr Remnant 2 is not bad, but certain aspects hold it back from being a direct upgrade from the first game. I'd encourage picking this game up if it's on sale, but I cannot bring myself to recommend it at full price. Hopefully future DLC and updates will bring more content and potentially fix the more glaring issues.

I've tried my absolute best to like this game but I just don't. This game does meta game progression / secrets / gunplay / classes and weapon variety very well, but it does so much more wrong.

[list]
[*]The character feels insanely stiff, making combat very clunky. Getting hit once is almost a death sentence because it's nearly impossible to get away from enemies and you'll get stunlocked if enemies surround you. This sucks even harder on boss fights that summon adds.
[*]The level designs are extremely poor and are so maze-like. This game is the ultimate "where the fuck am I supposed to go?" simulator.
[*]Boss fights vary from "Okay that was pretty cool" to "What the fuck whoever designed this needs to be shot"
[*]Literally everything is cryptic and barely explained. This game requires you to be checking the Wiki constantly because the game is nearly impossible to play without it. Pretty much every area, item, and mechanic is a puzzle with vague hints of what to do.
[*]Maps feel like a chore to walk through, especially if you're trying to figure out where the hell you're supposed to be going. The minimap doesn't even have cardinal directions on them so it's possible to accidentally end up walking south when you really meant to be walking north.
[*]Everything in this game feels [i]slow[/i]. Using items and consumables feels like a challenge because your animations are slower than enemies attacks, so you will get interrupted if you don't time them just right. The same goes with reloading guns.
[*]There are many unlocks that are available only through multiplayer mechanics. If you don't have anyone to play with to specifically aim for them, there are some things you won't be able to get.
[*]Ammo starvation is real. If you're on a big map or during some boss fights, it's entirely possible to run out of ammo. There are consumables to restore it (which as I said above, consumables take forever to use) and you can get ammo drops, but it's pure RNG if that happens.
[*]Replayability is questionable. When you start a new campaign or adventure mode, it's a dice roll of which version of the map you roll and the optional dungeons are also always random. If you're hunting for a specific armor / ring / weapon / amulet, you'll basically need to keep rolling the dice over and over until you get the map you want. The main areas and boss fights stay the same, so it can become repetitive quickly.
[/list]

Remnant II is one of those games that just keeps getting better the more you play it.

I originally enjoyed it for the combat and co-op for over 200 hours on my PS5, but coming back to it and actually digging into everything has made me appreciate just how much is hidden in this game. There are entire archetypes, weapons, armor sets, bosses, puzzles, alternate rewards, and areas that you can completely miss. Even after you think you've cleared a world, there's a good chance you've barely seen everything it can generate.

The randomized worlds are probably my favorite part. Rerolling doesn't just mean running the exact same content again with enemies shuffled around. Different storylines, dungeons, bosses, events, and secrets can appear, so exploration actually feels rewarding. I've had plenty of moments where I found something and immediately wondered, “How the f*ck was I EVER supposed to know this was here?” ....  and I mean that as a compliment.

Co-op is where the game really shines for me. Exploring with friends, finding some bizarre hidden passage, solving a puzzle together, or accidentally discovering an item none of you knew existed is exactly the kind of multiplayer experience I want. It's cooperative without turning the game into an MMO or forcing PvP into the experience.

It's not perfect. Some secrets cross the line from “cleverly hidden” into “there is absolutely no f*cking way I would've figured that out without looking it up,” and the menus/crossplay systems could definitely be explained better. But those annoyances haven't stopped me from wanting to see what's behind the next door.

If you like Souls-style combat but also love exploration, secrets, buildcrafting, loot, and co-op, Remnant II is absolutely worth playing.

[h1] Sidestep rather than a step forward. [/h1]

For every little thing Remnant 2 does or expands upon, there is a glooming dark side that drags the whole experience to a [b] NEUTRAL [/b] level. 

1. Story telling – We get more cinematics, character expositions and dialogue options, compared to the first game. Sounds great right? Yeah... if the writing was actually good. Most of the female characters are typical "Strong Women" whereas "Player" character is just a wimpy "do the dirty work" kinda individual. I have no problem with having strong female characters if you let me role play "MY" character the way I see fit. 
There are some plot holes in the story and literally every world is [b] HOSTILE [/b]. Even though on occasion player is welcomed as a saviour by friendly high ranking NPC's. You would think they would tell everyone else not to attack their "saviour" but nope...

2. We get more BIOMES and ENEMY TYPES! Yes, yes we do BUT.... Maps are too big and vertical so exploring them is a chore. It is especially frustrating if you try to figure out a way to get to the ledge above or below and when you finally get there... There's [b] NOTHING [/b]. In Remnant 1 you could find 1 Trait book and 1 Ring/Amulet per Map. This trend seems to follow to Remnant 2 with occasional extra item on top. 
Be ready to Backtrack A LOT. Which is not fun especially so, if you have to kill the same enemies over and over again. 
ENEMY A.I is frustratingly bad. They can glitch through walls still able to hit the player, they can stand still and do nothing while their buddies are trying to kill you, they can SPAWN behind the player IN CLOSE PROXIMITY WITHOUT MAKING ANY SOUNDS, they have badly telegraphed grab attacks and DELAYED COMBO ATTACKS worthy of ELDEN RING bosses. Seriously F those flying squid enemies. 
There is a JUMP action but it's triggered automatically when performing dodge over the gap in the ground. This combined with horrible vertical maps killed me more than anything else in the game. Just make a seperate button for jumping and let players decide how FAR they want to push forward ! 

Environmental traps are INSTA KILL now, so that's the second biggest reason for my death count . None of them are fun, especially when combined with clunky controls ( running, crouching and jumping ). I dread to play Hardcore Character with 1 life in Remnant 2... There is much more to be said but I have more important points to make so, let's move on.
3. Balancing. Many reviewers have mentioned that Balancing is very good in Remnant 2. That they coulnd't make a broken 1 hit K.O build and they always had to interact with the game mechanics rather than rely on the build itself.

Here's the thing. Remnant 1 was a power fantasy. I really enjoyed discovering or making and OP build. Going back and trashing the boss that gave me a hard time first playthrough. It was fun. If I wanted more challenge I would crank up the difficulty to Hard or Nightmare. They gave the player a choice on how they wanted to play the game.

Remnant 2 throws the power fantasy away. I uprade my weapons and other damage boosting mods.... only to deal the same pitiful damage as I was before the upgrade. Enemies still die in 3 body shoots even though the numbers are getting bigger. That's on Normal Difficulty while loading a new zone. If this wasn't bad enough, there is PLENTY of Boss encounters that feel absolutely UNBALANCED. You can either steam roll the boss first try or be swarmed by projectiles, trash mobs, AOE and elites while fighting the boss.... What were they thinking?! Ain't got stamina or healing on that matter to deal with such hectic fights. Eventually I beat the boss but It didn't feel like it was my skill but rather a bit of RNG luck. 

[b] Armours, Potions [/b] all recieved a NERF. You may no longer stack 60 minute potions on top of each other. Armours are reduced to FLAT damage reduction stats. Which in turn means "Fashion" only. New "Archtypes" or character classes are nothing more than cut content. In previous game everyone could level up all the traits albeit it took a long time to do so. The dev team separated the perks into classes and added some skills and bonuses to each one. Max trait lvl is now 85. That means you can't have useful bonuses like running speed etc. If you want to max your damage. Point being : Player character never feels poweful unlike in the first game. 

Weapons and Mods range from WHY IS THIS EVEN IN THE GAME?! There is SO SO MUCH GARBAGE in the game that I honestly preffer the deliberate loot of the first Remnant. Why use Rusty Lever Gun if you have a "Normal one" ? Why so many handguns with similar performance ? Why normal melee weapons don't have "perks" or mods only boss weapons have them? You got a cool ring? Nice... but it comes with a debuff. I started with a Hunter Class and pretty much played with a LEVER GUN AND REVOLVER THE WHOLE TIME. Maybe I was unlucky with the weapons I found but it was a dull experience.

4. Bugs and FPS drops. There is a lot and some of them progression breaking too. From enemies glitching to visual and audio bugs... The game has it all. Some are more annoying than others but to say it doesn't affect the joy of playing the game would be a lie. 

5. They said they have improved melee... I think I failed to notice then because aside from some fancy animations some weapons have, melee still feels like an AFTERTHOUGHT. Given the large amount of flying enemies and the fact that players can easily be staggered... Melee doesn't feel good or better than what we had in the first game.

6. BS deaths. The amount of times I died due to enemies literally spawning behind me, or jump didn't activate or some teleporting squid that doesn't make any noise decided to grab me from behind is ridiculous. Bugged out enemies inside the walls or WHEN THE ELITE DIES and his body despawns ANY ENEMY INSIDE THE DEAD BODY IS IMMUNE TO DAMAGE. Trying to run away by climbing a ledge? NOPE. Smallest of attacks can cancel your animation. Good luck in tight areas like sewers. Most enemies have "armour" on them so even if you empty the full clip of M60 to their head, they won't stagger. 

7. Economy is terrible. You need EVEN MORE scrap than in the first game. This seriously hampers the experimentation. I was constantly upgrading one – two weapons because I didn't want too use precious materials on a "new" weapon in hopes that its good. I did try most of the guns eventually, but decided to stick to what "works" for most of the scenarios. 

I am exhausted by playing this game. As much as I was enjoying the first one.... the changes they made in the second one are for the worse in my opinion. Instead of expanding on a good formula they made the game tedious to play. Bigger doesn't mean better. 

I will have to admit though that ART DIRECTION ( world, weapon, creature Designs ) are fantastic . They just need to hire someone better to do the map layout.

Let's start with the pros:
$50 price tag - In an era where most AAA games are being pushed out for $70 with additional $10-20 worth of "live service" battle passes and content this game is not only economical but you still get everything. The higher cost editions simply unlock content early.

No Live Service - mentioned above this game has a clear ending. Yet it retains it's replay-ability with the systems they created. There's reasons to go back to worlds using the adventure mode. There's procedural generated content that randomizes the game enough to make it easy to come back to.

Great co-op - While the game can be played single player it's also got 3 man co-op which is quite fun.

Souls-like light - The game has a lot of systems people who enjoy the Dark Souls style games will enjoy. It's less punishing by not removing your currency on death. Also since enemies are procedurally generated there's less memorization regarding levels and areas. Though memorization still matters regarding enemy move sets there's less emphasis on it overall. Otherwise difficulty is in enemy damage, your survive-ability, and ammunition conservation.

Graphics/Aesthetics - The graphics are great and the different area's all have their own distinct feeling. Unlike some games where there's visual confusion with everything going on I have never really had that kind of problem with this game. Aesthetically the area's all fit very well into what they are meant to be.

Show Don't Tell - For the most part the developers have adopted this approach to the game's lore and items. It rewards exploration and investigation. There's a reason there's an inspect item option and usually will lead you to secret locations and rewards. If you see a door you can't open it's usually a shortcut, take a moment to explore the area and you'll be rewarded.

Randomization - They built replay-ability into the game in a great way. When one boss has potentially 4 different rewards based on what you do before the boss fight as well as during the fight there's great reasons to go back to fight that boss. Alternate rewards besides usually bosses can have alternate move sets as well making the fight different from before.

Cons:
Mechanics - Some of the mechanical issues with the game are tied to various things. I like the Sci-Fi area of N'Erud aesthetically for what it portrays but mechanically it's open area's aren't implemented as well as the other worlds. Some of the materials you receive simply aren't used in amounts close to how you receive them while others are used far too much yet you barely get them.

Story - Overall the story is fine, while I listed Show Don't Tell as a pro for the game at the very end of the game it lacks critical exposition for the ending. Which is kind of disappointing.

3 Man co-op - I enjoy the co-op but this game like a great many has adopted the 3 man co-op rule. When you have 4-5 friends all playing at the same time this usually leaves someone out.

Armor - Armor plays a role but not as much as accessories. It'd be nice for a transmog type system to be implemented at some point so you can look a certain way while retaining the benefits of the armor of your choice.

At this point they can create DLC in the game in the form of new archetypes, new worlds to explore, and new weapons. If they do this I can easily see myself throwing money at them for it.

- No in-game voice chat
- No in-game text chat

So, you're stuck with gestures (hold down "G") and the pinger system when you play with random people online, which is a bit sad. Also, as of writing this, you can't add any random contacts to your friends over the game interface either, so there's a constant "invisible barrier" if you play the game online with random people. Usually the people you meet in the game are very kind, though matchmaking might take up to hour or two for someone to pop online, so you can often end up pretty much solo exploring even if you leave your game open as pubic.

As for bugs, nothing too major apart from occasional freezes on loading screens and crashes whenever someone joins or leaves your party, etc.

Other than that, it's a great-looking, fast paced shooter that requires a lot of reflexes and coordination, really testing your capabilities as a player (in terms of action, think of Helldivers 2 in the more challenging modes), where you also have to put your wit to good use in terms of  using your resources and ammunition wisely.
